{{Short description|Infinite graph without small cliques}}
{{unsolved|mathematics|Do the Henson graphs have the [[finite model property]]?}}

In [[graph theory]], the '''Henson graph''' {{math|''G''<sub>''i''</sub>}} is an undirected [[infinite graph]], the unique countable [[homogeneous graph]] that does not contain an {{mvar|i}}-vertex [[clique (graph theory)|clique]] but that does contain all {{mvar|K<sub>i</sub>}}-free finite graphs as induced subgraphs. For instance, {{math|''G''<sub>3</sub>}} is a [[triangle-free graph]] that contains all finite triangle-free graphs.

These graphs are named after C. Ward Henson, who published a construction for them (for all {{math|''i'' ≥ 3}}) in 1971.<ref name="henson">{{citation
 | last = Henson | first = C. Ward
 | journal = [[Pacific Journal of Mathematics]]
 | mr = 0304242
 | pages = 69–83
 | title = A family of countable homogeneous graphs
 | volume = 38
 | year = 1971
 | doi=10.2140/pjm.1971.38.69| doi-access = free
 }}.</ref> The first of these graphs, {{math|''G''<sub>3</sub>}}, is also called the '''homogeneous triangle-free graph''' or the '''universal triangle-free graph'''.

==Construction==
To construct these graphs, Henson orders the vertices of the [[Rado graph]] into a sequence with the property that, for every finite set {{mvar|S}} of vertices, there are infinitely many vertices having {{mvar|S}} as their set of earlier neighbors. (Only the Rado graph has such a sequence.) He then defines {{math|''G''<sub>''i''</sub>}} to be the [[induced subgraph]] of the Rado graph formed by removing the final vertex (in the sequence ordering) of every {{mvar|i}}-clique of the Rado graph.<ref name="henson"/>

With this construction, each graph {{math|''G''<sub>''i''</sub>}} is an induced subgraph of {{math|''G''<sub>''i'' + 1</sub>}}, and the union of this chain of induced subgraphs is the Rado graph itself. Because each graph {{math|''G''<sub>''i''</sub>}} omits at least one vertex from each {{mvar|i}}-clique of the Rado graph, there can be no {{mvar|i}}-clique in {{math|''G''<sub>''i''</sub>}}.

==Universality==
Any finite or countable {{mvar|i}}-clique-free graph {{mvar|H}} can be found as an induced subgraph of {{math|''G''<sub>''i''</sub>}} by building it one vertex at a time, at each step adding a vertex whose earlier neighbors in {{math|''G''<sub>''i''</sub>}} match the set of earlier neighbors of the corresponding vertex in {{mvar|H}}. That is, {{math|''G''<sub>''i''</sub>}} is a [[universal graph]] for the family of {{mvar|i}}-clique-free graphs.

Because there exist {{mvar|i}}-clique-free graphs of arbitrarily large [[chromatic number]], the Henson graphs have infinite chromatic number. More strongly, if a Henson graph {{math|''G''<sub>''i''</sub>}} is partitioned into any finite number of induced subgraphs, then at least one of these subgraphs includes all {{mvar|i}}-clique-free finite graphs as induced subgraphs.<ref name="henson"/>

==Symmetry==
Like the Rado graph, {{math|''G''<sub>3</sub>}} contains a bidirectional [[Hamiltonian path]] such that any symmetry of the path is a symmetry of the whole graph. However, this is not true for {{math|''G''<sub>''i''</sub>}} when {{math|''i'' > 3}}: for these graphs, every automorphism of the graph has more than one orbit.<ref name="henson"/>
